hook: The joke is in the title, and the article commits to it harder than you'd expect. Read it as a document losing a fight with its own anomaly: the effect is happening to the text in front of you. It's short, so go slowly enough to enjoy how the sentences bend.
whyItMatters: This is meta humor in its purest form: the anomaly is not an object in the file but something done to the file. Instead of describing an effect, it performs one, so you experience the cognitohazard rather than being told about it. Even the class header has been bent to fit the gag, which shows how far the familiar template can be pushed.
thingsToNotice:
Watch the compulsion escalate: the procedures and description slip the reference in fairly politely, but the survey summary turns into a parade of invented library hazards, from Dewey radiation given off by damaged patrons to restraints for people with overdue books. It gets darker than it first seems, because Agent Casey is fatally wounded by something in the building's hazardous waste pit, and the report can only explain it by pointing out, again, what the building used to be. The conclusions then collapse into a loop that says the same fact five ways and nothing else.

The real twist sits underneath the comedy. Nobody can describe what the building was used for between 1988 and 2004, the fire broke out the day the effect began, and the compulsion is exactly what keeps anyone from saying more, so the gag is also the cover-up.
